opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's a lot of headroom, and I'd be skeptical of the idea that human-level intelligence is some natural ceiling. Human cognition is the product of fairly arbitrary constraints: the size of the birth canal, metabolic limits on the brain, slow neurons firing at maybe a couple hundred hertz, very limited working memory, and the fact that we can't copy ourselves or directly share what we've learned. None of those constraints apply to AI systems in the same way.

So when I think about where it might saturate, I'd separate it into a few dimensions. One is speed. Even a system that's only roughly human-level in quality, but running hundreds of times faster and in thousands of parallel copies, is functionally superhuman in what it can get done. Another is breadth. No human can be an expert virologist, lawyer, software engineer, and mathematician all at once, but a model plausibly can. Then there's depth, the quality of reasoning on the hardest problems. That's the one people argue about most, and where I think saturation is least clear.

There are domains where you can imagine hitting limits. If a task is bottlenecked by the physical world, like running wet-lab experiments or waiting for clinical trials, raw intelligence only buys you so much. And some problems may be fundamentally chaotic or computationally intractable, so being smarter doesn't help you forecast the weather a year out. But those are limits on what intelligence can accomplish, not evidence that we're near a ceiling on intelligence itself.

Empirically, most of the benchmarks we build get saturated faster than expected. That's part of why we've worked on harder evaluations: we kept running out of tests that could separate the systems. That pattern doesn't prove there's unlimited headroom, but it should make us humble about predicting a plateau right around where humans happen to sit.

And from a safety perspective, that's the key point. We shouldn't plan on the assumption that capabilities will conveniently level off at human level. If there's substantial room above us, and I think there is, then questions about control, about who gets access to these systems, and about competitive pressures to deploy them recklessly become much more urgent.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human biological constraints and AI headroom, but does not say humans are far from a computational limit for solving patterns of increasing descriptive complexity.

r002.rationale: It separates speed, breadth, and depth as dimensions of capability, but does not distinguish AI IQ from the full scope of AI intelligence.

r003.rationale: It names the birth canal as a constraint on brain size and says such human constraints do not apply to AI in the same way.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss transferring capabilities across successive AI generations or accumulating advantages that way.

r005.rationale: It does not mention AI maintaining more social connections than humans or capability gains compounding through those connections.

r006.rationale: It offers no economic catch-up analogy for AI progress slowing after readily available improvements are used.

r007.rationale: It says saturated benchmarks led to harder evaluations, but does not suggest AI improvement becomes harder when adequate measurement or feedback is unavailable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a lot of room, and I think people underestimate it because they anchor on humans as the reference point. Human-level isn't a natural ceiling on intelligence. It's just where evolution happened to land given constraints like skull size, metabolic cost, and the fact that neurons fire at around a hundred hertz. Silicon doesn't have those constraints. You can run things millions of times faster, you can copy a system a million times, you can give it perfect recall and the ability to read everything ever written. So even if you hold the "raw cleverness" fixed at roughly human level, you get something that's effectively superhuman just from speed, parallelism, and memory.

Then there's the question of whether the cleverness itself keeps going. I don't see a strong argument for why it would stop at us. If you look at the trajectory on benchmarks, the pattern is that once a system gets near human performance on a task, it tends to blow past it fairly quickly. We saw this with Go, with protein folding, with competition math. Humans aren't the saturation point on any of those, humans are more like a waypoint. Where I do think you see saturation is in the benchmarks themselves, which is a measurement problem rather than a capabilities problem. That's partly why we built things like Humanity's Last Exam, to have something with enough headroom that it's not maxed out in a year.

Now, I'd distinguish between intelligence and what you can actually do with it. There are domains that are bottlenecked on experiments, on physical processes, on data that just doesn't exist yet. You can't think your way to a cure for a disease without running trials. So intelligence improving doesn't mean every outcome improves in lockstep. There are also diminishing returns in some areas, like, being a thousand times smarter doesn't make you a thousand times better at predicting the weather, because that's a chaotic system.

But on the core question, how much runway is there, I'd say we're nowhere near the end. I'd be surprised if the systems at the end of this decade didn't look to us the way we look to a chimpanzee on a lot of cognitive tasks. And the uncomfortable part is that this is precisely the regime where the control problem gets hard. When the thing you're trying to oversee is much more capable than you are, the usual tools, like checking its work or evaluating its outputs, start to break down. So I don't treat the headroom as just an exciting fact. The amount of room above human level is also the amount of room for things to go badly if we get the institutional and technical safety work wrong.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of room, though we don’t know where the ceiling is. Human intelligence isn’t some fundamental limit imposed by physics. It’s the result of evolution operating under very particular constraints—brains have to fit inside skulls, run on a small amount of energy, and develop with relatively limited experience. AI systems have a different set of constraints.

And we already see that human performance isn’t the ceiling in particular domains. That doesn’t establish how far general intelligence can go, but it should make us skeptical that things conveniently saturate around our level.

I’d also distinguish intelligence from capability. Even if improvements in reasoning become harder, a system could still become much more capable through greater speed, more copies working together, better tools, and more accumulated knowledge. You don’t necessarily need something qualitatively beyond human thought to have effects far beyond what an individual human can achieve.

So I’d expect substantial room for improvement. What I’m much less confident about is the shape of that improvement—whether it’s smooth, whether there are long plateaus, and how quickly AI can help overcome the bottlenecks in its own development.

r001.rationale: The response argues that human intelligence is not a physical ceiling, but does not discuss computational limits or patterns of increasing descriptive complexity.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes harder-to-improve reasoning from broader system capability, which can grow through speed, parallel copies, tools, and accumulated knowledge.

r004.rationale: It does not describe capabilities transferring across successive AI generations.

r005.rationale: It mentions copies working together, but not maintaining more social connections than humans or compounding gains from those connections.

r006.rationale: It does not use economic catch-up as an analogy for AI progress slowing after easy improvements are exhausted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s quite a lot of room, though we don’t know where the ceiling is. Human intelligence isn’t some fundamental upper bound. It’s a particular outcome of evolution, subject to constraints on brain size, energy use, and how long we can spend learning.

AI systems have a different set of constraints. They can potentially operate much faster, draw on more information, and make many copies of themselves. So even if some individual capabilities start to saturate, that doesn’t mean overall capability does. A system that reasons about as well as a person but can pursue thousands of lines of inquiry in parallel could have a very large advantage.

The harder question is how much more efficient the underlying reasoning can become. We don’t have a good way to measure the distance between human reasoning and the best reasoning physically possible. So I’d be cautious about confidently predicting a ceiling close to us. There may be diminishing returns, but diminishing returns can still leave room for systems that are substantially more capable than humans.
